titleBlock.headline: Genetics vs. Dietary Restriction: 960 Genetically Diverse Mice Reveal Resilience & Immune Trade-Offs of Extreme Fasting and CR
titleBlock.authors: Di Francesco, A., Deighan, A.G., Litichevskiy, L., Chen, Z., Luciano, A., Robinson, L., Garland, G., Donato, H., Vincent, M., Schott, W., Wright, K.M., Raj, A., Prateek, G.V., Mullis, M., Hill, W.G., Zeidel, M.L., Peters, L.L., Harding, F., Botstein, D., Korstanje, R., Thaiss, C.A., Freund, A. & Churchill, G.A.
titleBlock.summary: In a landmark Jackson Laboratory study of 960 genetically diverse female Diversity Outbred (DO) mice randomized across 5 feeding regimens—Ad Libitum (AL), 1-day/week fasting (1D IF), 2-day/week fasting (2D IF), 20% caloric restriction (20% CR), and 40% caloric restriction (40% CR)—genetic background explained ~3x more variance in lifespan (23.6%) than diet (~7.4–8.4%). While 40% CR extended median lifespan by +36.3% (+9.2 months), it induced lean mass loss and immune vulnerability, and the longest-lived animals were those that retained body weight and immune stability under stress.

studyOverview.title: The Question
studyOverview.content: Most rodent longevity studies use a single inbred strain (like C57BL/6J), masking how genetic diversity shapes response to caloric restriction (CR) vs. intermittent fasting (IF). In a genetically diverse population resembling humans, how do graded CR and IF compare, and do classic metabolic improvements (weight loss, lower glucose) actually predict how long an individual lives?

studyOverview.title: What They Did
studyOverview.content: Randomized n = 960 genetically unique female Diversity Outbred (DO) mice at 6 months of age into 5 lifelong dietary groups (~192 mice/arm): Ad Libitum (AL), 1 day/week fasting (1D IF), 2 consecutive days/week fasting (2D IF), 20% daily CR, and 40% daily CR, tracking 198 longitudinal clinical phenotypes (DEXA body composition, indirect calorimetry, glucose/insulin, hematology, FACS immune profiling, frailty, and grip strength).

studyOverview.title: What They Found
studyOverview.content: Lifespan scaled with restriction intensity: AL (25.4 mo) < 1D IF (28.0 mo, +10.2%) < 2D IF (28.5 mo, +12.2%) < 20% CR (30.5 mo, +20.1%) < 40% CR (34.6 mo, +36.3%). Crucially, genetics explained 23.6% of lifespan variance vs. ~7.4–8.4% for diet. Furthermore, metabolic health and lifespan were decoupled: mice that lost the most weight or adipose tissue on CR/IF died earlier, whereas stress resilience (retaining weight during handling), intact lymphocyte proportions, and low RDW predicted exceptional longevity.

dietArms.label: Ad Libitum (AL Control)
dietArms.bodyComposition: Progressive mid-to-late-life adiposity gain; preserved lean mass until late senescence.
dietArms.metabolicEffect: Baseline fasting glucose and respiratory quotient (RQ).
dietArms.immuneHematology: Standard age-related decline in naive T/B lymphocytes and gradual rise in RDW.
dietArms.tradeOffs: Higher baseline incidence of metabolic syndrome and earlier median mortality (25.4 months).

dietArms.label: 1-Day/Week Fasting (1D IF)
dietArms.protocol: 24-Hour Complete Fast Every Wednesday (Ad Libitum 6 Days)
dietArms.bodyComposition: Minimal net body weight reduction; preserved lean muscle mass.
dietArms.metabolicEffect: Cyclic weekly ketogenesis and RQ flexibility (rapid switch between fat oxidation during fast and lipogenesis on refeed).
dietArms.immuneHematology: Mild erythroid stress during fast-refeed cycles; preserved lymphocyte counts.
dietArms.tradeOffs: Modest median lifespan gain (+2.6 months) without requiring chronic daily calorie counting.

dietArms.label: 2-Day/Week Fasting (2D IF)
dietArms.protocol: 48-Hour Consecutive Fast Every Wed–Thu (Ad Libitum 5 Days)
dietArms.bodyComposition: Moderate cyclical weight fluctuations; preserved lean mass better than 40% CR.
dietArms.metabolicEffect: Pronounced 48-hour ketosis and improved fasting glucose, but large refeeding metabolic swings.
dietArms.immuneHematology: Elevated red blood cell distribution width (RDW) and erythroid instability from repeated 48-hr starvation-refeeding.
dietArms.tradeOffs: Failed to extend lifespan in mice that had high pre-intervention body weight prior to starting 2D IF at 6 months.

dietArms.label: 20% Caloric Restriction (20% CR)
dietArms.protocol: 2.75 g/day Chow Delivered Daily (~20% Below AL)
dietArms.bodyComposition: Balanced reduction in visceral adiposity with substantial preservation of lean body mass and bone mineral density.
dietArms.metabolicEffect: Robust improvement in insulin sensitivity, fasting glucose, and metabolic flexibility.
dietArms.immuneHematology: Preserved lymphocyte-to-myeloid balance and attenuated age-related rise in RDW.
dietArms.tradeOffs: Optimal healthspan-to-lifespan balance (+5.1 months median lifespan) without the severe immune or lean-mass penalties of 40% CR.

dietArms.label: 40% Caloric Restriction (40% CR)
dietArms.protocol: 2.06 g/day Chow Delivered Daily (~40% Below AL)
dietArms.bodyComposition: Severe loss of both fat mass and lean skeletal muscle mass; chronic hypothermia (lower body temperature).
dietArms.metabolicEffect: Lowest fasting glucose and chronic torpor/energy conservation, but decoupled from individual within-group survival.
dietArms.immuneHematology: Significant depletion of B lymphocytes, effector T cells, and lymphoid organ mass—increasing vulnerability to acute infection.
dietArms.tradeOffs: Maximized laboratory lifespan (+9.2 months median; ~1/3 lived >38 months) but at the cost of lean mass loss, cold intolerance, and immune suppression.

varianceBreakdown.description: Genetic ancestry across the 8 founder strains of Diversity Outbred mice accounted for nearly 3x more variation in lifespan than the dietary interventions.

varianceBreakdown.factor: Dietary Restriction Regimen (AL vs. IF vs. CR)
varianceBreakdown.description: While diet shifted population median survival by up to +36.3%, individual response within every diet arm spanned >25 months due to genetic variation.
Individual resilience trajectories best captured longitudinally by hematological (RDW), immune (lymphocyte %), and stress-weight-retention biomarkers.

keyFindings.title: Genetics Dominates Diet (~3x Greater Lifespan Variance)
keyFindings.desc: Additive genetic heritability explained 23.6% of total lifespan variance across the 960 mice, compared to ~7.4–8.4% explained by dietary restriction regimens.

keyFindings.title: Metabolic Biomarkers Are Decoupled From Lifespan
keyFindings.desc: Within any dietary group, lower fasting glucose, lower body weight, or reduced metabolic rate did NOT predict longer life—showing that metabolic health and intrinsic biological aging are distinct axes.

keyFindings.title: Stress Resilience & Late-Life Adiposity Retention Predict Survival
keyFindings.desc: Mice that maintained their body weight and fat reserves during phenotyping/handling stress lived significantly longer than mice that lost excessive weight under caloric restriction.

keyFindings.title: RDW and Lymphocyte Percentage Are Top Longevity Predictors
keyFindings.desc: Across all 198 phenotypes measured, low red blood cell distribution width (RDW—erythrocyte uniformity) and high circulating lymphocyte proportions were the strongest longitudinal predictors of remaining survival.

conclusions.title: Moderate CR (20%) Beats Extreme CR (40%) for Translational Healthspan
conclusions.content: While 40% CR achieved the longest laboratory lifespan (+36.3%) in pathogen-free cages, its severe depletion of lean muscle mass and adaptive immunity makes moderate 15–20% CR far safer and more translatable to free-living humans.

conclusions.title: Avoid Excessive Weight & Lean Mass Loss in Late Life
conclusions.content: The finding that weight retention under stress and late-life adiposity positively correlate with survival warns against aggressive caloric restriction in older or frail individuals.

conclusions.title: Routine CBC Biomarkers (RDW & Lymphocyte %) Track Resilience
conclusions.content: Two inexpensive metrics on any standard human Complete Blood Count (CBC)—low RDW and preserved lymphocyte percentage—emerged as more powerful predictors of longevity than fasting glucose or body weight.

protocolImplications: Translational takeaway: When implementing caloric restriction or intermittent fasting in humans, 'more weight loss' does not equal 'more longevity.' Moderate caloric restriction (10–20%, as validated in CALERIE™) or 1-day/week time-restricted/intermittent fasting captures longevity benefits while preserving lean skeletal muscle and immune competence. Track standard CBC resilience markers—specifically Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW < 12.5%) and Absolute/Percent Lymphocytes—alongside DEXA appendicular lean mass.
